title: Research
text:
Trustworthy data first. Machine learning can only be as reliable as the data it learns from, and that is where our work began. Sequencing experiments carry hidden quality problems: we showed that poor-quality samples that are unevenly distributed between patient groups, a quality imbalance, distort the results of a large share of published clinical RNA-seq studies (Genome Biology, 2024). We develop machine-learning tools that assess data quality automatically, building on seqQscorer, and release open benchmark datasets for quality control of next-generation sequencing. In the Einstein Foundation–funded project Erring Rigorously, we now introduce controlled errors in the wet lab to measure how they propagate into downstream analyses.
Models that learn biology. On the modelling side, we train and critically test foundation models for biological sequences, from DNA language models to transfer learning across peptides, metabolites and proteins. Rather than assuming that scale solves everything, we ask what these models actually learn, where standard architectures fall short, and which training objectives and benchmarks can do better. Where predictions should inform biology or the clinic, we favour interpretable models. Biologically informed neural networks such as MiracleNet tie their predictions to known genes and pathways, for example to predict survival in lung cancer from microRNA data. Our applications come from close collaborations in immunology, cancer and vascular biology, such as the vascular-ageing project SVITER.
Responsible and open. Generative models that can design DNA also bring new risks. Together with partners from AI, the life sciences and policy, we develop safeguards for AI-driven biological sequence design: our defence-in-depth framework in Nature Communications (2026) proposes layered protections across data, models and DNA synthesis, and our perspective in Trends in Genetics weighs innovation against risk in genomic AI. We share code, models and datasets openly on GitHub and Hugging Face, holding back only what would pose a biosecurity risk, such as training code for viral sequence models. And because the next generation of researchers will need to work across these boundaries, we are building new teaching formats, starting with the AIxBio: Frontiers and Futures curriculum project.

title: Ayşe Nur Sevilmiş
text:
I’m currently doing my M.Sc. in Bioinformatics at Saarland University and working as a research assistant at Universitätsmedizin Mainz on machine learning models for the immune system. My focus is on protein language models for antibodies and T-cell receptors.



Antibodies and T-cell receptors come from similar genetic processes, and have separate, domain-specific language models. Our current project tests whether knowledge carries over between domain-specific protein language models and how knowledge is captured in them in a benchmark against general-purpose protein language models.

title: Laurenz Kammeyer
text:
My name is Laurenz, I’m 26 years old, and I’m currently pursuing my Master’s in Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence. In my free time, I enjoy working out, playing tennis and the piano, as well as volunteering as a firefighter. When I originally chose my degree, it was a close race between Computer Science and Physics. Ultimately, I decided to go with CS because of its hands-on accessibility. I consider myself a creative and curious person, so it was important to me to be able to actively develop my own ideas in my chosen field. While major breakthroughs in physics nowadays often require expensive labs and highly specialized equipment, in IT, you can build world-changing projects with just a laptop and a GitHub account. Driven by this passion for innovation, I am excited to contribute to the team’s research.



Right now, I’m looking into how effective current AI safety methods are when applied to generative models in biology. Specifically, my research focuses on finding ways to prevent these models from generating harmful material. The goal is to modify the models so they can no longer be used to create, extend, or complete dangerous genetic sequences. To keep things entirely safe and avoid any exposure to actual toxic sequences, I am conducting my research using a proxy dataset made up of harmless enzymes.

title: Hassan Ahmed Hassan
text:
Hassan is a part-time PhD student in the Sprang Lab, working on large-scale models trained on DNA and RNA that can serve as general-purpose tools for biology. He and Max met in 2024 through the OpenBioML open-science community and have worked together on DNA language models ever since, more recently extending that work to the biosecurity of AI. The aim of his project is models that advance fundamental research into genome function while also powering applied work such as early cancer detection and zoonotic disease surveillance. Safety runs through the core of the project, with a focus on making models that are reliable, interpretable, and resistant to misuse. Alongside his PhD, Hassan works full-time as a Senior Data Scientist at Hippo Digital in the UK, with clients in the healthcare sector.

title: Welcome to the Sprang Lab
text:
Welcome to the Sprang Lab — the BioAI group at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz. This is where we share our research, code, and ideas in computational biology.
The blog is written by the whole group. Lab members, external students, and alumni are welcome to post about their work, for example a recent paper or a finished thesis, either on their own or together with me. The workflow is simple:

Fork the repository
Create a new folder under blog/posts/ named YYYY-MM-DD-your-title/
Write your post as index.qmd
Open a pull request

We look forward to sharing our work here. Stay tuned!

title: A defence-in-depth strategy for AI-driven sequence design, now in Nature Communications
text:
Generative AI models can now write biological sequences: proteins, enzymes and even small viral genomes. This opens real opportunities for medicine and biotechnology, from faster design of therapeutics to bespoke phages against antimicrobial resistance. The same capability could also be misused. Our Perspective in Nature Communications, published on 19 November 2026, sets out how the field can keep the benefits while managing the risks.
The paper grew out of the Wübben Sandpit conference on generative AI for biological sequences, a three-day workshop held from 25 to 27 November 2025 and funded by the Wübben Stiftung Wissenschaft. Twenty participants from molecular biology, AI, bioinformatics, biosecurity, ethics, medicine and policy, coming from academia, industry and government in Europe and the United States, mapped the dual-use risks of sequence design and drafted recommendations to address them. The work was led from the Department of Dermatology at the University Medical Center Mainz and the Institute for Quantitative and Computational Biosciences (IQCB) at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz.

title: A defence-in-depth strategy for AI-driven sequence design, now in Nature Communications
text:
What we propose
Our central argument is that no single safeguard is enough. Instead, protection should be layered along the whole chain from a digital design to a physical molecule, a “defence in depth”:

Data. A shared definition of what counts as dual-use pathogen data, more awareness among researchers of the risks in the data they hold, and tiered access instead of a simple choice between open and closed: foundational data stay open, while functional data on pandemic pathogens require verified credentials. Funders should check biosecurity risks when they review projects that will generate sensitive data.
Models. Risk–benefit assessment across a model’s whole lifecycle, from training to deployment; safety benchmarks that combine computational red-teaming with experimental validation; and hosted, API-based access for the most capable models, so that they can be audited independently and their weights are not distributed freely.
DNA synthesis. Stronger sequence screening across synthesis providers, customer identity checks and tracking of critical equipment, clear and binding rules for screening, and a sector-wide fund for research on risks and their mitigation.

At the same time, we argue against blanket restrictions. There is currently no evidence that AI can design entirely new, more dangerous human pathogens; the concern is about future, more capable models. Safeguards should therefore rest on a realistic view of what today’s models can and cannot do, so that they support responsible research rather than slow it down. Many of them, such as better interpretability and structured risk assessment, should make the models more useful as well. In our view, good governance is part of what makes progress possible.

title: Giorgia D’Amico
text:
I am an M.Sc. student in Applied Bioinformatics and a student research assistant at JGU Mainz, working at the intersection of AI and biology.



My project investigates how AI can learn and generate biological DNA sequences. Specifically, my research spans from alignment-free sequence analysis and learned genomic representations to the generative modelling of bacteriophage DNA, utilizing both autoregressive and diffusion-based approaches. By building reproducible pipelines for training, inference, and validation, I explore how AI can design diverse and biologically plausible phage genomes, opening new possibilities for synthetic genomics.

title: Giorgia D’Amico
text:
My project investigates how AI can learn and generate biological DNA sequences. Specifically, my research spans from alignment-free sequence analysis and learned genomic representations to the generative modelling of bacteriophage DNA, utilizing both autoregressive and diffusion-based approaches. By building reproducible pipelines for training, inference, and validation, I explore how AI can design diverse and biologically plausible phage genomes, opening new possibilities for synthetic genomics.

Papers with the lab

HA Hassan, G D’Amico, M Sprang. DVQ: A library for the visual and statistical representation of nucleotide sequences. Work in progress · github.com/sprang-lab/dvq

title: Yasmin Mansour
section: Project: Alternative polyadenylation as a marker of biological immune age
text:
Project: Alternative polyadenylation as a marker of biological immune age
As the human body ages, the immune system undergoes functional changes that can vary between individuals and across different immune cell types. This project aims to investigate whether alternative polyadenylation (APA), a mechanism involved in the regulation of messenger RNA processing, reflects age-related changes in immune cells and can be used to determine biological immune age.
To this end, single-cell transcriptomic data from different immune cell types will be analyzed, and machine learning approaches will be used to develop an APA-based “Immune Aging Clock”. Subsequently, the project will investigate how infections and vaccinations influence these age-associated APA patterns and whether such changes can be used to detect alterations in biological immune age.

title: Dr. Maximilian Sprang
text:
I am a computational biologist and, since August 2026, Independent Junior Group Leader for Bioinformatics and Genomics at the Department of Dermatology of the University Medical Center and the Institute for Quantitative and Computational Biosciences (IQCB) of Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, Germany, where I head the Sprang Lab (BioAI group). From 2027, I will take up a position as IQCB Scientist, the first appointment of this kind at the new institute. I am also Junior Faculty at the Max Planck Graduate Center (MPGC) Mainz and a PI in the Center for Synthetic Genomics Heidelberg–Karlsruhe–Mainz (Center SynGen). My research focuses on machine learning for genomics, with particular interests in DNA language models, data quality in multi-omics, and the biosecurity implications of generative AI in the life sciences. I am a father of two.
I maintain active international collaborations, including work with DeoxyTech Ltd. (Manchester, UK) on DNA embedding models, involvement in the OpenBioML open science community, and partnerships with researchers in Edinburgh, Barcelona and Zürich and across Europe on biosecurity and AI safety in biology.

title: Projects
text:
Spatiotemporal Atlas of Vascular Inflammaging and Therapeutic Targeting of DPP4 for Endothelial Resilience
SVITER asks whether an established class of diabetes drugs could help protect blood vessels as we age. The project centres on DPP4, an enzyme on the surface of endothelial and immune cells that cleaves, and thereby regulates, a broad range of inflammatory mediators such as interleukins, growth factors and cytokines. DPP4 inhibitors (“gliptins”) are approved, widely prescribed and well tolerated, and there is growing evidence that blocking DPP4 reduces senescence and oxidative stress in the vasculature. In earlier work, the partner group in Anesthesiology showed that the DPP4 inhibitor sitagliptin protected small blood vessels from inflammation-related dysfunction in patients undergoing major surgery, with similar effects in mice. The group has also shown that distinct subtypes of brain endothelial cells respond differently to inflammation.
Building on this, the project has three aims:

Map vascular ageing by building an integrated single-cell atlas of how endothelial cells change with age across 11 tissues and different vessel types.
Link cellular changes to outcomes by connecting these age-related changes to measures of vascular and organ health.
Test DPP4 as a therapeutic target by determining how much DPP4 contributes to vascular resilience during ageing, and whether DPP4 inhibitors could become a strategy against age-related vascular decline.

SVITER is a collaboration between our lab, which contributes the bioinformatics, and the group of Dr. Miriam Julia Renz at the Department of Anesthesiology.
Funding: ReALity Initiative, Rhineland-Palatinate · Period: 2026–2028 · PIs: Dr. Maximilian Sprang (Department of Dermatology, contact) and Dr. Miriam Julia Renz (Department of Anesthesiology), University Medical Center Mainz

title: Projects
text:
Erring Rigorously
On quantifying the impact of errors in the wet lab on downstream analysis
Sequencing data are the backbone of modern biomedical research, but technical artefacts and batch effects introduced at the bench can blur the biological signal and lead to wrong conclusions. In earlier work we showed that differences in data quality between sample groups, a quality imbalance, affect more than 30% of public RNA-seq datasets, including clinical studies (Genome Biology, 2024). Most of the field deals with such problems after the fact, by filtering or correcting the data. Erring Rigorously goes to their source and asks which steps in the wet lab actually introduce them, and how much each one matters.
To find out, we make mistakes on purpose. Starting from a clean ground-truth experiment, a treatment–control comparison of cells from the same stock under optimal conditions, we perturb the same workflow at defined stages:

Cell culture: higher passage numbers and different confluency at splitting
RNA: controlled degradation to different levels of RNA integrity
Handling: a parallel workflow run by a different person, to create a realistic batch effect
Library preparation: poly-A enrichment, rRNA depletion and long-read protocols




Planned design: a 4 + 4 ground-truth comparison of treatment and control, with each perturbation (cell passage, cell density, RNA integrity) added at two levels plus a batch effect, 64 samples in total


For every sample we measure quality with our machine-learning tool seqQscorer and follow the effect through differential expression analysis, to see which perturbations distort the biological signal and which leave it intact.
The project will produce a fully annotated, openly shared dataset that pairs a known biological comparison with known technical errors: a benchmark for testing batch-effect correction and normalisation methods, and for refining seqQscorer. It also tackles a broader question: does poor technical quality always rule out meaningful biological insight, or can imperfect data still be useful once its biases are understood? Wet-lab work is carried out with partner labs, while our lab leads the bioinformatics and machine learning.
Funding: Einstein Foundation Award for Promoting Quality in Research, Early Career category (2025) · Period: 2026–2027

title: Projects
text:
AIxBio: Frontiers and Futures
From shared blind spots to a new curriculum for teaching at the interface of AI and the biosciences



Participants of the workshop “AI in Bioscience: Converging Interests and Joint Solutions”, Mainz, October 2026


AI is changing bioscience research quickly, but computational and experimental scientists still often talk past each other: different research cultures, disciplinary boundaries and unsolved methodological problems get in the way of real collaboration. AIxBio: Frontiers and Futures starts from those open problems rather than from finished results, and turns them into teaching.
Workshop (October 2026). On 27 and 28 October 2026, the workshop “AI in Bioscience: Converging Interests and Joint Solutions” brought PhD candidates and postdocs from bioscience and AI together in Mainz with keynote speakers and industry representatives. Every participant contributed a “Blind Spot”: a dataset they don’t know how to model, or an algorithm still looking for a bioscience use case. These were presented as posters throughout the workshop and then taken up in small breakout groups, which worked through shared challenges such as biological data analysis, model validation and interpretability, and translating computational advances into experimental practice.
Student retreat (2027). Next year, a retreat takes the clustered blind spots, the breakout-group results and a literature search from the workshop, and translates the problems and solutions into the key skills the next generation of quantitative bioscientists will need. The goal is a community-driven white paper on the future of bioscience teaching and a concrete new curriculum.
The project is led by Max Sprang, with Nicole Johnstone (University of St Andrews, Scotland) as co-lead.
